'''bleak<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v.'' [< ''bleak''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.''; var. of ''bleach''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To make white or pale; bleach.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become white or pale.

'''bleak<sup>2</sup>''' (blēk), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''bleke'', dial. ''blick''; = Icel. ''bleikja'' = OHG. ''bleicha'', MHG. ''blicke''; from the adj. ''bleak'' (Icel. ''bleikr'', OHG. ''bleih''), from the pale color of its scales (see ''bleak''<sup>1</sup>). The synonymous term ''blay''<sup>1</sup>, < AS. ''blǣge'' = D. ''blei'' = G. ''bleihe'', is not directly connected with ''bleak''<sup>2</sup>.] An English name of a small cyprinoid fish, ''Alburnus lucidus''. Other forms of the name are ''bleik'', ''blick''. Also called ''blay''.

'''bleak<sup>3</sup>†''', ''v. t.'' [Var. of ''bleach''<sup>2</sup> and ''black'', ''v.''] To blacken; darken. ''Cotgrave.''

'''bleakish''' (blē′kish), ''a.'' [< ''bleak''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.] Moderately bleak; somewhat bleak.
{{smaller block|A northerly or ''bleakish'' easterly wind.
{{right|''Dr. G. Cheyne'', Ess. on Health.}}}}

'''bleakly''' (blēk′li), ''adv.'' In a bleak manner or situation: as, the wind howls ''bleakly''.
{{smaller block|Neere the sea-coast they ''bleakely'' seated are.
{{right|''May'', tr. of Lucan, ix.}}}}

'''bleakness''' (blēk′nes), ''n.'' [< ''bleak''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ness''.] The quality of being bleak; coldness; desolation: as, “the ''bleakness'' of the air,” ''Addison.''
{{smaller block|The landscape will lose its melancholy ''bleakness'' and acquire a beauty of its own.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Twice-Told Tales, II.}}}}

'''bleaky''' (blē′ki), ''a.'' [Extended form of ''bleak''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.''] Bleak; open; unsheltered; cold; chill. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|{{c|The ''bleaky'' top of rugged hills.}}
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Virgil’s Georgics, iii.}}}}

'''blearedness''' (blēr′ed-nes), ''n.'' [< ''bleared'', pp. of ''blear''<sup>1</sup>, + ''-ness.''] The state of being bleared or blurred with rheum. ''Holland.''

'''blear-eye''' (blēr′ī), ''n.'' [Rather from ''blear-eyed'', ''a.'', than from ''blear''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'', + ''eye.'' Cf. LG. ''bleer-oge'', ''plür-oge'', blear-eye, from the adj. See ''blear-eyed.''] In ''med.'', a disease of the eyelids, consisting in chronic inflammation of the margins, with a gummy secretion from the Meibomian glands; lippitude. Also called ''blear-eyedness.''

'''blear-eyed''' (blēr′īd), ''a.'' [< ME. ''blereyed'', ''blereighed'', etc., < ''bleren'', blear, + ''eye'', ''eighe'', eye; cf. Dan. ''plir-öjet'' = LG. ''bleer-oged'', also ''plür-oged'', blear-eyed, of similar formation. Cf. also LG. ''blarr-oged'', with noun ''blarr-oge'', due to confusion with ''blarren'', cry, howl, weep, = G. ''blarren'', ''blerren'', usually ''plärren'', roar, bellow, = E. ''blare''<sup>1</sup>; but there is no etymological connection. See ''blear''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Having sore eyes; having the eyes dimmed or inflamed by flowing tears or rheum; dim-sighted.
{{smaller block|Crook-back’d he was, tooth-shaken, and ''blear-ey’d.''
{{right|''Sackville'', Ind. to Mir. for Mags.}}}}
'''2.''' Wanting in perception or understanding; short-sighted.

'''blear-eyedness''' (blēr′īd-nes), ''n.'' Same as ''blear-eye.''

'''bleariness''' (blēr′i-nes), ''n.'' [< ''bleary'' + ''-ness.''] Blearedness.

'''blearness†''' (blēr′nes), ''n.'' [< ''blear''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'', + ''-ness.''] The state of being blear. ''Udall'', Mark x.

'''blear-witted''' (blēr′wit″ed), ''a.'' Dull; stupid.
{{smaller block|They were very ''blear-witted'', i’ faith, that could not discern the gentleman in him.}}

'''bleary'''<sup>1</sup> (blēr′i), ''a.'' [< ''blear''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Bleared; rheumy; dim: as, ''bleary'' red eyes.—'''2.''' Blurred; confused; cloudy; misty.
{{smaller block|<poem>Oh give me back my native hills,
If bleak or ''bleary'', grim or gray.</poem>
{{right|''Cumberland Ballad.''}}}}

'''bleary'''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'' See ''bleery.''

'''bleat''' (blēt), ''v. i.'' [< ME. ''bleten'', < AS. ''blǣtan'' = D. ''blaten'', ''bleeten'' = MLG. LG. ''bleten'' = OHG. ''blāzan'', MHG. ''blāzen'', G. dial. ''blässen'', ''blätzen'', bleat; cf. G. ''blöken'', bleat, bellow (see ''balk''<sup>2</sup>, ''bolk''), L. ''balare'', bleat (see ''balant''), Gr. βληχᾶσθαι, bleat, βληχή, Dor. βλαχά, a bleating: all perhaps ult. of imitative origin, like ''baa'', q. v.] To cry as a sheep, goat, or calf; also, as a snipe.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then suddenly was heard along the main
To low the ox, to ''bleat'' the woolly train.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Odyssey, xii.}}}}

'''bleat''' (blēt), ''n.'' [< ''bleat'', ''v.''] The cry of a sheep, goat, or calf; also, of a snipe.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''bleat'' of flocks, the breath of flowers.</poem>
{{right|''Moir'', Harebell.}}
<poem>And got a calf . . .
Much like to you, for you have just his ''bleat''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, v. 4.}}}}

'''bleater''' (blē′tėr), ''n.'' An animal that bleats; specifically, a sheep.
{{smaller block|<poem>In cold, stiff soils the ''bleaters'' oft complain
Of gouty ails.</poem>
{{right|''John Dyer'', Fleece, i.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|bleaching|583|bleed}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''bleaching''' (blē′ching), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''bleach''<sup>1</sup>.]   The art or process of freeing textile fibers and fabrics, and various other substances (such as materials for paper, ivory, wax, oils), from their natural color, and rendering them white, or nearly so. {{smaller|The ancient method of bleaching by exposing to the action of the sun’s rays, and frequent wetting, has been nearly superseded, at least where the business is prosecuted on a large scale, by more complicated processes in connection with powerful chemical preparations. Among these preparations, the chief are chlorin and sulphurous acid, the latter being employed more especially in the case of animal fibers (silk and wool), while cotton, flax, and other vegetable fibers are operated upon with chlorin, the bleaching in both cases being preceded by certain cleansing processes. Glass is bleached by the use of chemical agents, usually braunite, saltpeter, arsenious acid, and minium or red lead.}}

'''bleaching-liquid''' (blē′ching-lik″wid), ''n.'' A liquid for bleaching; specifically, blanching-liquor.

'''bleaching-powder''' (blē′ching-pou″dėr), ''n.'' A powder made by exposing slaked lime to the action of chlorin; chlorid of lime. {{smaller|It may be regarded as a mixture of slaked lime and a double salt of calcium chlorid and calcium hypochlorite. It is the principal agent used in bleaching textile fabrics, and is also a powerful disinfectant.}}

'''bleak'''<sup>1</sup> (blēk), ''a.''   [Also assibilated ''bleach'' (obs.), dial. ''blake'', q. v.; < ME. ''bleke'' (assibilated ''bleche'') (also ''bleike'', prob. due to Icel.), earlier ''blake'', ''blak'' (i. e., ''blāk'', different from ''blăk'', black, though to some extent confused with it), pale, wan, < AS. ''blāc'' (var. ''blǣc'', whence prob. ult. E. ''bleach''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'', q. v.), pale, wan, also bright, shining (= OS. ''blēk'', pale, shining, = D. ''bleek'' = MLG. ''blēk'', LG. ''blek'' = OHG. ''bleih'', MHG. G. ''bleich'' = Icel. ''bleikr'' = Sw. ''blek'' = Dan. ''bleg'', pale, wan), < ''blīcan'' (pret. ''blāc'', pp. ''blicen''), shine, = OS. ''blīkan'' = OFries. ''blīka'', shine, = D. ''blijken'' (pret. ''bleek''), appear, = Icel. ''blīkja'', ''blīka'', shine, = OHG. ''blīhhan'', shine (MHG. ''blīcan'', G. ''bleichen'', grow pale, mixed with weak verb ''bleichen'', bleach: see ''bleach''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''), akin to Skt. √ ''bhrāj'', shine, and perhaps to Gr. φλέγειν, burn, blaze, φλόξ, flame, L. ''flamma'', flame, ''fulgere'', shine, etc.: see ''flame'', ''fulgent'', ''phlegm'', ''phlox'', etc. Related E. words are ''blank'', ''blink'', ''bleach''<sup>1</sup>, perhaps ''black'', and ''bright''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1†.''' Pale; pallid; wan; of a sickly hue.
{{smaller block|With a face dedly, ''bleyk'', and pale. {{right|''Lydgate.''}}}}
{{smaller block|She looked as pale and as ''bleak'' as one laid out dead.
{{right|''Foxe'', Martyrs (Agnes Wardall).}}}}
'''2.''' Exposed to cold and winds; desolate; bare of vegetation.
{{smaller block|<poem>Say, will ye bless the ''bleak'' Atlantic shore?</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Cho. to Brutus.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Wastes too ''bleak'' to rear the common growth of earth.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth.''}}}}
{{smaller block|It is rich land, but upon a clay, and in a very ''bleak'', high, exposed situation. {{right|''Gray'', Letters, I. 258.}}}}
'''3.''' Cheerless; dreary.
{{smaller block|Her desolation presents us with nothing but ''bleak'' and barren prospects. {{right|''Addison.''}}}}
'''4.''' Cold; chill; piercing; desolating.
{{smaller block|<poem>Entreat the north
To make his ''bleak'' winds kiss my parched lips.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, v. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|The night was ''bleak'' ; the rain fell; the wind roared.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., ix.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become white or pale.

''bleihe'', is not directly connected with ''bleak''<sup>2</sup>.]   An English name of a small cyprinoid fish, ''Alburnus lucidus''. Other forms of the name are ''bleik'', ''blick''. Also called ''blay''.

{{smaller block|The landscape will lose its melancholy ''bleakness'' and acquire a beauty of its own.

'''bleaky''' (blē′ki), ''a.''   [Extended form of ''bleak''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'']   Bleak; open; unsheltered; cold; chill. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|{{c|The ''bleaky'' top of rugged hills.}}
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Virgil’s Georgics, iii.}}}}

'''blear<sup>1</sup>''' (blēr), ''v.''   [< ME. ''bleren'', make dim or rheumy, in reference to the eyes, esp. in the phrase ''blear one’s eyes'', i. e., deceive, hoodwink one; rarely intrans., blink; cf. Dan. ''blire'', also ''plire'', blink, = Sw. ''plira'', dial. ''blira'', and ''blura'', blink (cf. dial. ''blirra fojr augu'', quiver before the eyes, of summer heat), = LG. ''plüren'', ''plyren'', ''pliren'' (also ''bleer-'' in ''bleeroged'' = E. ''blear-eyed'', q. v.), blink; cf. G. dial. ''blerr'', an ailment of the eyes.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To affect (the eyes) with flowing tears or rheum so that the sight is dimmed and indistinct; make rheumy and dim: as, “''blered'' her eyes,” ''Piers Plowman.''
{{smaller block|<poem>To his ''bleared'' and offended sense,
There seems a hideous fault blazed in the object.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Tease the lungs and ''blear'' the sight.
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, iii.}}}}
'''2.''' To blur, as the face with weeping; obscure; obfuscate.
{{smaller block|Stern faces ''bleared'' with immemorial watch.
{{right|''Lowell'', Cathedral.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To blear one’s eyes†''', figuratively, to deceive; hoodwink; blind.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>They wenen that no man may hem bigile,
But by my thrift, yet shal I ''blere her eye.''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Reeve’s Tale, l. 129.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Entising dames my patience still did proue,
And ''blear’d mine eyes.''</poem>
{{right|''Gascoigne'', The Fruits of Fetters.}}}}

'''II.†''' ''intrans.'' To have bleared or inflamed eyes; be blear-eyed.

'''blear<sup>1</sup>''' (blēr), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [Not an orig. adj., but assumed from ''blear-eyed'', where ''blear'' is directly from the verb. See ''blear-eyed.'']   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Sore or dim from a watery discharge or other superficial affection: applied only to the eyes.
{{smaller block|A wit that can make your perfections so transparent, that every ''blear'' eye may look through them.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man in his Humour, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Half blind he peered at me through his ''blear'' eyes.
{{right|''Layard'', Nineveh and Babylon, i.}}}}
'''2.''' Producing dimness of vision; blinding. [Obsolete or poetical.]
{{smaller block|Power to cheat the eye with ''blear'' illusion.
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 155.}}}}
'''3.''' Dim; indistinct; confused in outlines. [Rare.]

'''II.''' ''n.'' Something that obscures the sight. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|Nor is the ''blear'' drawn easy o’er her e’e.
{{right|''A. Ross'', Helenore, p. 91.}}}}

'''blear<sup>2</sup>†''' (blēr), ''v.''   [< ME. ''bleren;'' origin obscure.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To thrust (out); protrude: with ''out.''
{{smaller block|[They] stood staring and gaping upon Him, wagging their heads, writhing their mouths, yea ''blearing out'' their tongues.
{{right|''Bp. Andrews'', Sermons, ii. 173.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To thrust out the tongue in mockery.
{{smaller block|He baltyrde, he ''bleryde'', he braundyschte ther-after.
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 782.}}}}

'''blearedness''' (blēr′ed-nes), ''n.''   [< ''bleared'', pp. of ''blear''<sup>1</sup>, + ''-ness.'']   The state of being bleared or blurred with rheum.   ''Holland.''

'''blear-eye''' (blēr′ī), ''n.''   [Rather from ''blear-eyed'', ''a.'', than from ''blear''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'', + ''eye.'' Cf. LG. ''bleer-oge'', ''plür-oge'', blear-eye, from the adj. See ''blear-eyed.'']   In ''med.'', a disease of the eyelids, consisting in chronic inflammation of the margins, with a gummy secretion from the Meibomian glands; lippitude. Also called ''blear-eyedness.''

''bleer-oged'', also ''plür-oged'', blear-eyed, of similar formation. Cf. also LG. ''blarr-oged'', with noun ''blarr-oge'', due to confusion with ''blarren'', cry, howl, weep, = G. ''blarren'', ''blerren'', usually ''plärren'', roar, bellow, = E. ''blare''<sup>1</sup>; but there is no etymological connection. See ''blear''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Having sore eyes; having the eyes dimmed or inflamed by flowing tears or rheum; dim-sighted.
{{smaller block|Crook-back’d he was, tooth-shaken, and ''blear-ey’d.''
{{right|''Sackville'', Ind. to Mir. for Mags.}}}}
'''2.''' Wanting in perception or understanding; short-sighted.

'''blear-eyedness''' (blēr′īd-nes), ''n.'' Same as ''blear-eye.''

'''bleariness''' (blēr′i-nes), ''n.''   [< ''bleary'' + ''-ness.'']   Blearedness.

'''blearness†''' (blēr′nes), ''n.''   [< ''blear''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'', + ''-ness.'']   The state of being blear.   ''Udall'', Mark x.

'''blear-witted''' (blēr′wit″ed), ''a.'' Dull; stupid.
{{smaller block|They were very ''blear-witted'', i’ faith, that could not discern the gentleman in him. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man out of his Humour, v. 2.}}}}

'''bleary'''<sup>1</sup> (blēr′i), ''a.''   [< ''blear''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Bleared; rheumy; dim: as, ''bleary'' red eyes.—'''2.''' Blurred; confused; cloudy; misty.
{{smaller block|<poem>Oh give me back my native hills,
If bleak or ''bleary'', grim or gray.</poem>
{{right|''Cumberland Ballad.''}}}}

'''bleary'''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'' See ''bleery.''

'''bleat''' (blēt), ''v. i.''   [< ME. ''bleten'', < AS. ''blǣtan'' = D. ''blaten'', ''bleeten'' = MLG. LG. ''bleten'' = OHG. ''blāzan'', MHG. ''blāzen'', G. dial. ''blässen'', ''blätzen'', bleat; cf. G. ''blöken'', bleat, bellow (see ''balk''<sup>2</sup>, ''bolk''), L. ''balare'', bleat (see ''balant''), Gr. βληχᾶσθαι, bleat, βληχή, Dor. βλαχά, a bleating: all perhaps ult. of imitative origin, like ''baa'', q. v.]   To cry as a sheep, goat, or calf; also, as a snipe.

To low the ox, to ''bleat'' the woolly train.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Odyssey, xii.}}}}

'''bleat''' (blēt), ''n.''   [< ''bleat'', ''v.'']   The cry of a sheep, goat, or calf; also, of a snipe.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''bleat'' of flocks, the breath of flowers.</poem>
{{right|''Moir'', Harebell.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And got a calf . . .
Much like to you, for you have just his ''bleat''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, v. 4.}}}}

'''bleater''' (blē′tėr), ''n.'' An animal that bleats; specifically, a sheep.
{{smaller block|<poem>In cold, stiff soils the ''bleaters'' oft complain
Of gouty ails.</poem>
{{right|''John Dyer'', Fleece, i.}}}}

'''bleaunt†''', ''n.''   [ME., also written ''bleeaunt'', ''blehand'', ''bliand'', ''blihand''; = MLG. ''bliant'' (with term. varied from orig.) = MHG. ''blīalt'', ''blīat'', < OF. ''bliaut'', ''bliaud'', ''bliat'', earlier ''blialt'' (mod. F. dial. ''blaude'', ''biaude'': see ''blouse'') = Pr. ''blial'', ''bliau'', ''bliaut, blizaut'' = Sp. Pg. ''brial''; ML. ''blialdus, bliaudus, blisaudus'', a kind of tunic; origin unknown.]   A garment common to both sexes in the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth centuries. {{smaller|As worn by women, it was a tunic placed over the chemise, usually with long and loose sleeves, and held by a girdle, except perhaps when a garment was worn above it. That for men was worn as an outer garment, and especially over the armor, in which case it is hard to distinguish it from the ''tabard'', which afterward replaced it. For mounted men it was divided nearly to the girdle, to enable the rider to sit in the saddle.}}
{{smaller block|A blewe ''bleaunt'' obofe brade him al ovir.
{{right|''King Alisaunder'', p. 167.}}}}
{{smaller block|Blysnande whyt watȝ hyr ''bleaunt''.
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), i. 163.}}}}

'''bleb''' (bleb), ''n.''   [Another form of ''blob'', q. v.]   '''1.''' A blister or pustule.—'''2.''' A bubble, as in water or other fluid, or in a substance that has been fluid, as glass.
{{smaller block|Arsenic abounds with air ''blebs''. {{right|''Kirwan.''}}}}

'''blebby''' (bleb′i), ''a.''   [< ''bleb'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Full of blebs, blisters, or bubbles.
{{smaller block|[Meionite] fuses . . . to a white ''blebby'' glass.
{{right|''Dana'', System of Mineral. (1868), p. 318.}}}}

'''bleck''' (blek), ''n.''   [Also (in def. 1) assibilated ''bletch''; < ME. ''blek, bleke'', appar. < AS. ''blæc'' (= Icel. ''blek'' = Sw. ''bläck'' = Dan. ''blæk'', ink), prop. neut. of the adj. ''blæc'', black: see ''black'', ''n.'']   '''1.''' Any black fluid substance, as black ink, blacking for leather, or black grease.—'''2.''' Soot; smut.—'''3†.''' A black man.—'''4.''' A local English name of the coalfish, ''Pollachius virens''.

[Now only prov. Eng. or Scotch.]

'''bleckbok''' (blek′bok), ''n.'' Same as ''bleekbok''.

'''bled''' (bled). Preterit and past participle of ''bleed.''

'''blee†''' (blē), ''n.''   [< ME. ''blee, ble, bleo,'' < AS. ''bleoh, blioh,'' usually contr. ''bleó, blió,'' color, hue, complexion, = OS. ''blī'' = OFries. ''blī, blie,'' North Fries. ''bläy,'' color.]   Color; hue; complexion.
{{smaller block|Thou art bryght of ''blee.''{{right|''Eglamour,'' l. 933.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I have a lemman
As bright of ''blee'' as is the silver moon.</poem>
{{right|''Greene,'' George-a-Green.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>White of ''blee'' with waiting for me
Is the corse in the next chambere.</poem>
{{right|''Mrs. Browning,'' Romaunt of the Page.}}}}

'''bleed''' (blēd), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''bled,'' ppr. ''bleeding.''   [< ME. ''bleden,'' < AS. ''blēdan,'' bleed (= OFries. ''blēda'' = D. ''bloeden'' = LG. ''blöden'' = OHG. ''bluotan,'' MHG. G. ''bluten,'' = Icel. ''blædha'' = Sw. ''blöda'' = Dan. ''blöde''), < ''blōd,'' blood: see ''blood,'' and cf. ''bless''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To void or emit blood; drop, or run with, blood: as, the wound ''bled'' profusely; his nose ''bleeds.''
{{smaller block|Many upon the seeing of others ''bleed'' . . . themselves are ready to faint, as if they ''bled.''{{right|''Bacon.''}}}}
'''2.''' Figuratively, to feel pity, sorrow, or anguish; be filled with sympathy or grief: with ''for'': as, my heart ''bleeds for'' him.
{{smaller block|Take your own will; my very heart ''bleeds for'' thee.
{{right|''Fletcher (and another),'' Queen of Corinth, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|I ''bleed'' inwardly ''for'' my lord.{{right|''Shak.,'' T. of A., i. 2.}}}}
